articles.headline: Israel is ‘disrupting entire ecosystems’, including Lebanon’s wheat crop
keyFacts: Israel's war on Lebanon damaged wheat production and left 24 percent of cropland abandoned, experts told Al Jazeera.
Researcher Mariam Ibrahim said wheat area losses in southern Lebanon reached 61 percent during the 2024-2025 season.
Experts warned that war destruction could prevent small farmers from rebuilding their livelihoods after the fighting ends.
body: Israel’s war on Lebanon has damaged the country’s wheat production and harmed the lives of farmers, experts told Al Jazeera.

For the last three years, Israel has been waging a war on Lebanon, where it has occupied large parts of the south and destroyed homes and infrastructure, in what some experts have said is a deliberate effort to make the land uninhabitable.

Repeated Israeli attacks have created havoc on the country’s wheat production, particularly in the south and in eastern Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, where lands abandoned due to the impacts of war have increased to around 24 percent.

“They’re disrupting entire ecosystems,” Munira Khayyat, author of A Landscape of War: Ecologies of Resistance and Survival in South Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “[Israel is] advancing the possibilities of drought and desertification, basically weakening the capacity of this land to hold life.”
Farmlands damaged

Since 2023, Israel has been attacking large swaths of southern Lebanon, including using chemicals like white phosphorus, in what analysts and locals said was an effort to make the ground sterile or uninhabitable. A ceasefire was brokered in 2024 by France and the United States, but Israel never stopped attacking targets in Lebanon.

On March 2, Israel escalated its war on Lebanon for the second time in under two years. Hezbollah had attacked Israel following Israel’s assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei two days earlier. The group also said it was in response to near-daily ceasefire violations by Israel.

Since then, Israel has reinvaded southern Lebanon, taking land up to 10 kilometres (6.2 miles) inside the country. Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-brokered framework agreement in June, which was supposed to put into motion so-called “pilot zones”. Under these pilot zones, Israeli troops would withdraw to be replaced by the Lebanese Armed Forces, who would also work to disarm Hezbollah.
Instead, Israeli troops have continued to level destruction in southern Lebanon, detonating homes and crucial infrastructure, including farmland.

“The South [of Lebanon] experienced the highest average losses [in wheat-growing areas], reaching 47 percent in 2023-2024 and 61 percent in 2024-2025,” Mariam Ibrahim, a researcher with Lebanon’s National Council for Scientific Research [CNRS-L] and author of a recent paper called “Wheat in Crisis” that tracked Lebanon’s wheat struggles from 2017 to 2025, told Al Jazeera. “The Bekaa plain, which accounts for approximately 64 percent of Lebanon’s national wheat production, was also significantly affected, losing around 43 percent and 57 percent of its wheat area during the two respective seasons.”
In areas like the border town Bint Jbeil, 100 percent of cropland was destroyed, while in the Baalbeck district to the east, the study says approximately 32 percent of cropland was destroyed.
Wheat price influences
Ibrahim said the Russian-Ukrainian war led to an increase in bread prices and incentivised some domestic Lebanese production.

“The depreciation of the Lebanese pound meant that farmers could potentially generate higher revenues and profits in local currency when selling their wheat, as wheat prices were increasingly influenced by international market prices,” she said. “This provided an additional economic incentive to expand wheat cultivation, and our results showed that Lebanon’s wheat cultivation area reached its peak [during] the 2022-2023 season.”

However, experts said that since 2023, Israel’s war on Lebanon led to the proportion of land that had been used to grow wheat that was now left fallow increasing from 9 percent to 24 percent, mostly in the south and the Bekaa Valley.

Elias Ghadban, a food security expert with the independent Beirut-based consultancy firm AgriDev, told Al Jazeera that the destruction of land used to farm wheat has not made a “significant difference” at the national level, but it has had a damaging effect on southern wheat farmers who “lost their livelihoods”.
Ghadban also pointed to the fact that the cost of living has increased in Lebanon while salaries have failed to match that increase. “The expenditure on basic needs went up,” he said.

The economic crisis, followed by three years of war, has devastated many farmers, particularly as much of southern Lebanon’s farmland is largely unindustrialised. Experts warn that the destruction caused by Israel’s war could prevent many farmers from rebuilding their livelihoods, even after the fighting ends.

“All those small farmers who have made southern Lebanon what it is today and have been able to hold that land through their attachment to it, through their farming of it, through their existential need to be on that land in order to make their lives viable, that’s going to be broken,” Khayyat said.

articles.headline: Hell Let Loose's original developers' Napoleonic-era extraction game, Hunger, gets December early access release, and an open beta this month
keyFacts: Developer Good Fun Corp announced that the extraction game Hunger will enter Steam early access on December 3.
An open beta for the game is scheduled to take place from November 27 to November 29.
Hunger features a melee-focused combat system set in an alternate history, plague-ravaged version of Europe.
body: Good Fun Corp, the studio made up of the original developers behind Hell Let Loose, has finally announced a release date for its anticipated next project: Hunger. The extraction shooter-slasher game enters early access on Steam on 3rd December, and there's good news if you're eager to try it out before then.

Hunger's first and only open beta has also been announced, taking place 27th-29th November, the weekend prior to its early access launch. Unlike past tests, this one is available for anyone who requests access on Steam.

Though it may appear as yet another extraction shooter on the surface, Hunger offers more complex and intertwined systems than most. For one, combat has a focus on melee with only a few intentionally clunky firearms available. Though this is a PvPvE game, the vs environment side includes the sort of puzzle-solving, questing and dungeon-raiding typical of RPGs. The game's alternate history, plague-ravaged European setting gives it a grimey, steel-and-mud look few games have.

Beyond the in-match experience, Good Fun's ambitions extend to Hunger's MMO-style progression, its hub area with distinct characters and varied playable classes - all of which can be sampled in the upcoming beta.

Hunger just came off a very successful closed beta, which clearly didn't suffer by kicking off right alongside Modern Warfare 4's DMZ early access. Hunger is currently among Steam's most-wishlisted games, with over 700,000 wishlists, according to the developer.

The launch version includes three large maps, six playable characters, and five Mastery trees with more than 100 Masteries to unlock for your characters. Hunger has only been announced for PC so far, but will presumably arrive on consoles following its early access journey.

articles.headline: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why
keyFacts: ZDNet reports that migrating from Ubuntu to Fedora is a manageable process because both distributions share many similarities and user-friendly features.
Fedora generally offers faster application startup times and provides more current software versions compared to Ubuntu, according to the article.
While both systems use the GNOME desktop environment, Fedora provides a stock experience, whereas Ubuntu customizes its interface to resemble the older Unity layout.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Migrating from Ubuntu to Fedora is less stressful than you think.
- The similarities between the two distributions outweigh their differences.
- Both distros are great, but experiencing something new is a joy.

In the world of Linux, distro hopping is practically a spectator sport. At some point, we get bored with the distro we’re using and decide to try something new. Perhaps there’s a distro that offers better features, works with more hardware, or has a larger support community. There are so many reasons for switching distros.
Also: Ubuntu 26.04 vs. Fedora 44: My verdict

However, for those new to Linux, the idea of leaving behind a distribution that’s been working just fine can be daunting, especially when you’re considering jumping to a distribution that isn’t as familiar and uses different technology.
More from ZDNET

As a new Linux user decades ago, I started with Caldera Open Linux 1.0 and immediately jumped to Red Hat Linux 5.2 (before Red Hat became Fedora). I stayed with Red Hat for years, until I found Ubuntu (I believe it was version 4).
Back then, making the jump wasn’t nearly as easy as it is now; in fact, it was unnerving. I was so used to how Fedora did things that I wasn’t certain I’d be able to acclimate.

But I did! And then, after realizing that hopping from one distro to another wasn’t the end of the world, I hopped around for a few years, from distro to distro until I settled back on Ubuntu-based distributions.
Also: Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next
They’re very similar

First, let’s get the obvious out of the way: Ubuntu and Fedora are both Linux. It’s not like you’re jumping from Windows or MacOS to Linux. This is a lateral move, which is not nearly as fear-inducing.

Beyond that, Ubuntu and Fedora are much more similar than you might expect. They both have GUI tools for everything you need; they’re both secure; they both have great package managers and package manager front-ends; they both make it easy to install all of the software you need (and all of the software you need is readily available); and they’re both user-friendly.
Also: 5 of my favorite Linux distros for AI – and why

If you get beyond the GUI and dip your toes into the command line, they both (mostly) use the same commands. Yes, there are some variations, but when you’re first learning the CLI (if you ever do — it’s not necessary), you’ll find those basic commands on Ubuntu are exactly the same as they are on Fedora.
Fedora is faster

If you migrated from Windows to Ubuntu, you’ve already experienced what a faster operating system feels like. If you jump from Ubuntu to Fedora, you’re going to experience that again, because Fedora is (somewhat) faster than Ubuntu. The difference might not be as exaggerated as it was when you went from Windows to Linux, but it is noticeable. Animations are faster, apps open faster, and switching between desktops is faster — nearly every aspect of Fedora is a bit faster than in Ubuntu.
I’ve tested several aspects with regard to the speed of Ubuntu and Fedora, and here are my conclusions:
Boot time

This is almost a tie. When rebooting from a logged-in desktop to the login screen, Fedora took 13.69 seconds, while Ubuntu took 14.31 seconds. The only caveat to that is if Fedora has updates that require a reboot, in which case Fedora takes considerably longer. The only time you have to reboot Ubuntu after an update is if the kernel is upgraded.
Application startup

Fedora wins this one, especially when it comes to Flatpak and Snap apps. Snap apps simply cannot compete with the speed of Flatpak apps (more on this in a bit). I tested this by opening a Snap app on Ubuntu and a Flatpak app on Fedora, using GIMP (since I know GIMP takes a while to start). On Fedora, the Flatpak GIMP took 3.48 seconds, and on Ubuntu the Snap app version of GIMP took 4.34 seconds.
App installation

This is one area where Ubuntu has a slight edge, but only when installing via the default package manager (rather than Flatpak or Snap). I tested this by timing the installation of Audacity using each package manager (DNF5 and APT) from the command line. DNF5 installed Audacity in 15.34 seconds, whereas the Ubuntu installation took 14.61 seconds.
Fedora is fresher

Generally speaking, Fedora not only ships with newer apps than Ubuntu, but it also gets updates faster than Ubuntu. That’s not to say that Ubuntu uses out-of-date packages; rather, Fedora is more cutting-edge than Ubuntu.
Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for
At the same time, that doesn’t mean Fedora uses unstable applications. All software that ships and/or is updated on Fedora is well-tested and stable — it’s just fresher.
Flatpaks versus Snaps

Flatpaks and Snaps are universal package managers. Fedora ships with Flatpak, and Ubuntu is all-in on Snaps. While these two technologies have the same goal (making software installation easier and more secure), they take different approaches.

First off, Flatpak was created by Red Hat, while Snap was created by Canonical. Snap is partially proprietary, while Flatpak is fully open-source. Flatpak enforces mandatory sandboxing, whereas Snap makes sandboxing optional. Flatpak apps launch faster than Snap apps. Finally, Snap packages are automatically updated, whereas Flatpak apps require manual updates.
Also: My favorite GNOME-based Linux distros
Overall, Flatpak is widely considered the superior technology by the Linux community.
In my experience, Flatpak is a better technology for the desktop, whereas Snap is best suited for servers.
GNOME = GNOME (sort of)

If you were to look at both Ubuntu and Fedora, you would swear they use different desktop environments. Au contraire, mon ami. Both Fedora and Ubuntu use GNOME; the difference is that Ubuntu customizes GNOME to look more like the Ubuntu Unity UI Canonical tested back in 2010. Since then, Ubuntu adopted GNOME and customized it so it wouldn’t irk users who had grown accustomed to Unity.

Fedora, on the other hand, sticks with a stock installation of GNOME for its flagship release. The good news is that, if you like the Ubuntu take on GNOME, you can install the necessary GNOME extensions (the main one being Dash to Panel) to get a similar layout. You can also get the Unity-like top bar by installing the Unite-Shell extension.

articles.headline: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro does not like to be taken apart
keyFacts: iFixit gave the new touchscreen MacBook Pro a 5 out of 10 repairability score after conducting a teardown.
Specialists praised the easily removable lid but noted that internal components like USB-C ports and fans remain difficult to access.
The display panel cannot be replaced individually because attempting to separate it from the lid causes the glass to crack.
body: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time.
Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go.
The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal.

Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration.

The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for.
Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places.

That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory.
Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds.
For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit , but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro.

The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal.
Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones.
The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®

articles.headline: Trump’s ex-lawyer Alina Habba loses whopping $50M contract after president blasted ‘outrageous’ deal
keyFacts: Concord Partners terminated former Trump attorney Alina Habba Mildon's $50 million general counsel contract, citing a failure to perform duties.
The firing followed President Trump's public criticism of her deal with the family of a pardoned Venezuelan billionaire.
A person close to Habba Mildon said she plans to pursue legal action over her termination.
body: President Trump’s former personal lawyer Alina Habba Mildon has lost a $50 million contract with the family of a pardoned Venezuelan billionaire — days after the commander-in-chief blasted the arrangement as “obnoxious and outrageous.”

Habba Mildon was fired by Concord Partners, a Florida-based company established by the daughter of Venezuelan banker Julio Herrera Velutini, according to a Nov. 4 letter obtained by the New York Times.
The company cited a “failure to perform duties” in terminating the former Trump attorney, who had been guaranteed more than $50 million over four years to serve as Concord’s general counsel.
A person close to the Herrera family told the Times that Habba Mildon’s priorities appeared to shift after she began dating Turkish investor Turhan Mildon, whom she married in September.
Habba Mildon will reportedly get to keep the $8 million signing bonus and another $6.5 million in payments she had already received.
The contract called for her to receive $10 million in annual payments, along with additional bonuses.
Habba Mildon declined to comment on her termination to the Times, but a person close to her said she was planning on pursuing legal action.
The stunning split comes after Trump publicly torched the arrangement last month, saying he had told his former attorney he did not want her receiving the money.
“I told her, and I said, ‘I don’t want her paid,’” the president added, claiming he had someone speak to the people behind the deal.

Trump also reportedly told aides and allies that the Herrera family should stop paying Habba Mildon and suggested she donate some of the money to his future presidential library or another Trump-related entity.
The eye-popping contract raised questions about the timing of Habba Mildon’s business arrangement and the Herrera family’s efforts to secure a presidential pardon for its patriarch.

Alina Habba signed the agreement in late October 2025, while serving as an acting US attorney for New Jersey. She began working with Concord Partners on Jan. 1, 2026, while serving as a senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi.

Herrera, who had faced federal bribery charges stemming from an alleged scheme involving Puerto Rico’s governor, reached a plea deal in August 2025, pleading guilty to a misdemeanor campaign finance violation.
Trump granted Herrera a full and unconditional pardon on Jan. 15, 2026, two weeks after Habba Mildon began working for the family-backed company.
Habba Mildon has denied any wrongdoing, insisting her employment had nothing to do with securing the pardon.
“Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the DOJ — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false,” she previously said.
The former Trump lawyer, who served as the president’s personal attorney before joining the Justice Department, has also faced scrutiny over her time as New Jersey’s top federal prosecutor.
A federal appeals court ruled that she had been unlawfully serving in the role, ultimately forcing her to resign in December 2025.

articles.headline: Trump wanted little Kei trucks for America, Toyota makes it happen
keyFacts: President Trump previously requested that the Department of Transportation legalize Japanese Kei cars for the United States market.
Toyota announced it is reviving the Scion brand to experiment with unconventional vehicle concepts like the KEI-01.
Kei cars are small, fuel-efficient vehicles restricted by Japanese government regulations on size, engine capacity, and power output.
body: The idea that Americans should be offered a greater choice of smaller cars has support from strange bedfellows indeed. After all, who could forget President Trump—usually one to take a maximalist approach to any problem—announcing last year that he wanted the Department of Transportation to make Japan’s diminutive “Kei” cars legal here in the US.

Ars’ attempts to get DoT to tell us more about the potential influx of little vehicles have mostly fallen on deaf ears. But this week, there has been movement on the topic, with Toyota announcing that it will bring back the Scion brand with the KEI-01.
What’s a Kei car?

Here in the US, the preponderance of humongous SUVs is a consequence largely of government policies, specifically corporate average fuel economy standards that made it less profitable to sell smaller, efficient cars. Japan’s Kei cars are what happens if the government instead restricts the size, engine capacity, and power output.

A Kei car must fit within the following dimensions: 11.2 feet (3.4 m) long, 4.9 feet (1.5 m) wide, and 6.6 feet (2 m) tall, with an engine displacement of no more than 0.66 L and an output of 63 hp (47 kW) or less. That’s a far cry from the more than 16 feet (4.9 m) of a full-size pickup truck, but it makes sense for a country where you’re not allowed to buy a car unless you have somewhere to park it, with those spaces being at an absolute premium.

Being affordable to buy and economical to run sure doesn’t hurt either, and last year, Japan bought almost 1.7 million Kei cars, out of total sales of 4.6 million vehicles. Depending on where you live in the US, it can be varying degrees of difficult to import a Kei car, at least until now.
Scion is back?

Toyota killed off its Scion sub-brand more than a decade ago, ending the haggle-free approach and cars aimed at younger buyers in favor of selling more Toyotas. But now it’s back as “Scion by Toyota,” which the automaker will apparently use to experiment with less traditional ideas. But forget about a cool-but-boxy EV in the mold of the Honda N-One or Nissan Sakura.

articles.headline: Brazil electoral court fines Meta, sees no deliberate election bias
keyFacts: Brazil's top electoral court fined Meta 7.5 million reais for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month's presidential election.
The court stated that Meta lacked transparency and missed deadlines, though it found no evidence of deliberate actions to influence the election.
Meta strongly denied the ruling and stated it will defend itself against false allegations in ongoing legal proceedings.
body: Brazil's top electoral court has ordered Meta to pay 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month's presidential election.
However, the judicial body has so far found no evidence that Meta deliberately acted to influence the election outcome.

Ahead of the runoff vote on October 25, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's coalition filed a complaint, accusing Meta of "algorithmic manipulation" favoring his far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro.
Platforms owned by Meta include Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
Meta told the court last month that it had implemented measures to guarantee equal treatment for both campaigns.
Meta lacked transparency, court says
The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) unanimously ruled on Tuesday to impose the 7.5 million reais fine on the US tech giant.
Meta missed deadlines and lacked transparency in its investigation, the court said.

On the other hand, the court's reporting judge Marco Aurelio Belizze wrote in his ruling that there were no preliminary evidence indicating that any intentional actions were taken to influence the election.
"That conclusion would require robust evidence, to be produced through the appropriate legal proceedings," he said.
According to Bellizze, the fine was based on Meta's overall handling of the court orders, including delays, incomplete disclosures, and challenges in verifying some of the information it provided.
In a statement on Wednesday, Meta strongly denied the court's ruling.
"We will continue to present the facts and defend ourselves against false allegations in the ongoing legal proceedings," Meta said in a statement on Wednesday.
Lula vows to rein in social media
Lula defeated Bolsonaro in a tight run-off in October 25 with him winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.2%.
In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race.
"We had to overcome foreign interference in the election, coming from outside through digital platforms that we will have to regulate," he said.

articles.headline: Europe wants to ban 'dark patterns' in apps and loot boxes for minors
keyFacts: The European Commission proposed the Digital Fairness Act to ban harmful practices like dark patterns, loot boxes for minors, and unclear pricing.
Companies violating these new consumer protection rules could face fines of up to six percent of their annual global revenue.
The proposal aims to centralize enforcement powers to better investigate large-scale cases and improve coordination across European member states.
body: Europe wants to ban 'dark patterns' in apps and loot boxes for minors
Tech companies in breach could face fines up to six percent of their global revenue.

Europe just released a proposal for a new set of consumer protection rules called the Digital Fairness Act (DFA), the EU Commission wrote in a news release. The bloc is targeting practices that harm children and push people into spending more, including things like unclear pricing, addictive design features, ads aimed at minors and "dark patterns" like hard-to-cancel subscriptions. The penalty for non-compliance could be up to six percent of a company's annual revenue, according to the draft copy.

"Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services, not on their ability to exploit consumers or their ability to evade the rules," said EU justice chief Michael McGrath in a statement. "We are not making it harder to do business, we are making it harder to do business unfairly."

The act seeks to protect consumers in a number of ways, like banning dark patterns, forcing clear and transparent online pricing for cultural and sports events and allowing consumers to turn off "addictive design features that encourage excessive or compulsive spending. It would also restrict unfair practices that encourage overspending by minors, like pay-to-win in games (loot boxes) and persistent prompts.

The DFA also addresses influencer marketing, requiring transparency from content creators about commercial content. It would also take on unfair personalized ads and prices that target minors, while putting an end to "subscription traps" that are difficult to cancel.

The EC also proposed to shift enforcement power from member states to a more centralized system. It would give the Commission direct powers to investigate large-scale cases with a major impact on consumers, speed up and improve coordination with member states and strengthen enforcement against non-EU companies.

This could be seen as an attempt to remove the patchwork of enforcement that currently happens around Europe in countries like France. It could also be an attempt to tilt regulatory power away from Ireland, a nation that hosts major tech giants including Apple, Google, Meta and Microsoft. A recent report from UN experts raised concerns about the independence of Ireland's privacy regulator, citing the risk of "undue influence" from tech firms hosted there.

articles.headline: Can Barack Obama be credited for the blue wave? Perhaps – but others fathered this success
keyFacts: Democrats regained majorities in the United States House and Senate following a recent election wave.
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed won election in Michigan to become the first Muslim senator in United States history.
The author attributes progressive candidate victories to the combined political influence of Barack Obama and Bernie Sanders.
body: A blue wave has surged in the United States. It has been a week since the Democrats hammered the Republicans and regained majorities in the House and the Senate, and the credit for that is, shall we say, a matter of debate.

Success has many fathers. One of them is Barack Obama, the first to break the kind of barriers a new generation of Democrats has overcome. This week, I follow what can and cannot be traced to the man who still holds a unique position in the liberal political imaginary, almost a decade after leaving the White House.

Barack Obama’s presidency and specifically his first election win, remains a formative politicising moment for many millennials. Few imagined that a Black man with an Arab Muslim middle name, and an electrifying agenda of hope, could become president of the United States. Then there were his own personal attributes: an orator for the ages, cool as ice, confident and unflappable. These qualities were sharpened by what followed – a Donald Trump presidency that wrecked political institutions and norms, fomented racial divides, led by a peevish, insecure narcissist that made the Obama years feel like a hallucination. The Trump era, and how the country swung so sharply in another direction, suggested that Obama was in fact, not the start of something, but an anomaly. But there may be more of an enduring legacy to Obama than the Trump era suggests.
A canny alliance

The question is: How much does a Dr Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s new senator and the US’s first ever Muslim senator, owe to Obama? El-Sayed answered that question himself by saying he is picking up the baton from the former president.

Obama also riffed on that note of continuity when he threw himself behind El-Sayed during the last days of the latter’s campaign, by comparing the Islamophobic attacks on El-Sayed’s name to those he faced. “I remind them his name was Barack,” El-Sayed said, of his detractors. He likened his disagreements with Obama to a son who loves his dad and “really appreciates all they’ve done, but … here are some things I would have done differently”.

But rewind a little, and this begins to look like clever campaigning. El-Sayed previously said that the Obama presidency had left the country “no better off”. He criticised Obama’s “war on terror” campaigns in Pakistan and Yemen, use of drones and for presiding over record deportations. Obama’s historic win, El-Sayed wrote, is a memory that “will serve not as a reminder of the history we made that night – but of the silly emotions of a naive young man who didn’t understand that hope and change required more than flowery prose and a winning smile”. Oof.

When questioned on these strong critiques, El-Sayed’s softer tone credited Obama with one specific and revealing achievement: being of a certain background and still believing that he could make it into high office.
A racial rather than political legacy

This suggests that Obama’s impact lies less in any radical anti-status quo politics that he pioneered – the sort that Bernie Sanders championed – but simply in breaking that psychological racial barrier for the American electorate. It is impossible to say whether successful candidates like Zohran Mamdani or El-Sayed would have prevailed in an environment steeped in Islamophobia, if Obama had not prevailed in an environment steeped with racism and Islamophobia. There is an argument that a president who was presented as radical, an “Arab”, even as a terrorist, who then spent eight years in the White House without passing sharia law, retained enough political muscle memory.

But is that all that new left-wing candidates of colour have to thank Obama for? It can be argued that Obama’s hawkish wars and conventional immigration policy, for example, preserved the sort of mainstream political capital that he could confer on people like El-Sayed. Since leaving office, Obama has remained a broadly milquetoast figure, occupying a cultural and political territory in which he has been refashioned as a curator of pop culture. From recommending literature and music, to his latest podcast, in which he hosts guests to discuss “great books”, Obama has frustratingly recused himself from the big political battles playing out since he left office, choosing to become some sort of jazz-playing uncle.

When he did make interventions, Obama’s once-moving rhetoric sounded remote and inappropriate for the moment. On Gaza, where a genocide is grinding down an entire population, Obama posted a weak statement which spoke of securing “lasting peace”, lacking the moral clarity to name the crimes that have been committed.
Cop-out or shrewd strategy?

This cop out reveals that Obama, even out of office and free to be a political engine of change without risk to his career in Washington DC, is not a cautious canny tactician. He is just that regular establishment centrist critiqued for being little more than flowery prose and winning smiles.

But when he showed up for El-Sayed, bringing his trademark humour and presence to the Michigan campaign, one could see how valuable that centrism was and that Obama does not flinch from defending and endorsing politicians with more progressive views than him. In choosing to show up, lending his imprimatur of authority to a candidate who has sharply criticised him while sitting firmly outside the Democratic party mainstream on everything from corporate power to Israel, Obama enabled El-Sayed to advance a revolutionary agenda.

But that agenda is no orphan either. It owes much to Bernie Sanders who ran for the Democratic presidential nomination twice on a left-wing platform, and since his loss, continued advancing positions such as reducing military spending, curbing corporate powers, blocking military sales to Israel and wealth taxes for billionaires. Much of the exciting politics in the blue wave is downstream from him.

Working in tandem with Obama’s backing, these legacies have paved the way for the success of the racial outsider and those who want to break the grip of ‘moderate’ establishment politics. Not many fathers, but two.

articles.headline: Why are fewer Black Americans getting GLP-1s?
keyFacts: Researchers found that Black patients were about 20 percent less likely than white patients to be prescribed newer diabetes drugs.
According to the CDC, about 12 percent of Black adults have diabetes, compared with roughly 7 percent of white adults.
The article notes that Black patients' diabetes was historically blamed on lifestyle rather than housing, food, financial, and healthcare inequities.
body: GLP-1s have become the newest celebrity miracle drug, with famous athletes like Serena Williams and Charles Barkley sharing that they’ve used it for weight loss.
Why are fewer Black Americans getting GLP-1s?
How race and disease have always been mistakenly intertwined.

Drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy have become a status symbol. But before they were famous, GLP-1s were developed to treat Type 2 diabetes, a disease that occurs when a person’s blood sugar becomes too high. It affects nearly 40 million Americans and hits Black Americans especially hard. According to the CDC, about 12 percent of Black adults have diabetes, compared with roughly 7 percent of white adults. Yet when researchers reviewed 26 studies from across the country, they found that Black patients were about 20 percent less likely than white patients to be prescribed newer diabetes drugs.

That gap has deep roots. A century ago, doctors called diabetes a “luxury disease” of wealthy white and Jewish people, and many didn’t believe Black people could get the disease at all. Even after the landmark 1985 Heckler Report exposed stark racial disparities in American health, Black patients’ diabetes was often blamed on lifestyle rather than on the housing, food, financial, and healthcare inequities shaping their health.

Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our series, Kahlil Explains, which unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the history of race and diabetes in America to unpack why Black patients are still less likely to get access to GLP-1s, and why closing that gap will take more than a prescription.

articles.headline: From Green Screen to Gray Box: AI Is Stepping Onto the Hollywood Sound Stage
keyFacts: Entertainment studio Promise Advanced Imagination is using gray boxes and AI to speed up film production and reduce costs.
Company officials state that AI tools assist human artists with backgrounds and lighting rather than replacing the creative roles of directors and actors.
Promise is currently testing this technology with Disney and has a series pilot in production with another studio.
body: On screen, a woman runs toward a cliff and peers anxiously over the edge, teetering as she looks down at a perilous mountain dotted with boulders, her hair flying in the wind.

She’s not, though. I can see her from where I’m standing in the middle of a Disney sound stage in Los Angeles. She’s standing in a “gray box,” a small, walled-off space on the studio floor, neutral-colored walls speckled with small cross marks for positioning. She’s next to a stack of blue-carpeted boxes that serve as a stand-in for whatever large prop that post-production decides to add in digitally later.
A camera is pointing at her, following her every move. And an almost instant rendering on a screen has placed her on that cliff, perfectly lit, wind tousling her hair, thanks in part to AI.
More from CNET

Green screens and blue screens have been used for more than half a century in TV and filmmaking, allowing post-production crews to insert visual effects and backgrounds behind the actors. But the bright hue can reflect onto objects and skin, and constant adjustments to the backdrop are needed when the director wants to switch to a new angle of the shot.

Filming in a gray box like the one I’m standing next to offers more flexible shots. And combining that with AI-generated or assisted backgrounds speeds up post-production, according to entertainment studio Promise Advanced Imagination, which showcased its filming product during the Disney Accelerator Demo Day last week.

Setting up shots takes less time in gray boxes than it does with a green screen background, Promise co-founder and chief creative officer Dave Clark told me, giving crews more time to be creative because “they’re not bogged down by having to take 2 to 3 hours to change the setup.”

“You’re able to still capture the right performance and the right blocking … this allows me to just focus on the story, focus on the creative and not worry,” Clark said. “You can get multiple takes because you can get them faster, you don’t have to worry about moving the crew, you don’t have to worry about changing lights, everything stays consistent so I can just focus on the story.”
Crews can save time while filming by using these gray boxes. More time (and cost) is saved during post-production by using AI tools to help fill in the backgrounds and replace lighting and objects.

While some environments are wholly AI-created, most are made by human 3D renderers and visual effects artists working with AI as one of their tools. Using AI to help fill in backgrounds lowers the cost of production but still ensures it has the size and scale of high-quality productions, Clark says, with production companies needing a lot less capital to produce pilots.
Clark, who’s also a director, insists that everything still “goes through the hands of human artists,” however.

“Much like Disney or Pixar, the process begins with the script, then it goes into storyboard and then (filming),” Clark said. “I think that traditional mindset and that traditional skill set that you only learn over decades of experience is really what amplifies this technology and lets it work for your creative capabilities.”

As filmmaking and animation studios increasingly explore the use of AI tools in streamlining productions, there have been concerns that human jobs will be removed, including across actors, animators, writers, set designers and more.

David Min, vice president of Disney Innovation, told me this system just fills in the background of movies, which is already done with other technologies, such as green screens. This just makes it easier and faster, since lighting changes can even be done in post-production. It means the people on set can focus just on the performances and direction. There will always be directors, writers and actors, he said.
Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro agrees, saying “technology itself is not the goal.”
“We’re being very aggressive about exploring emerging technologies,” D’Amaro said at the event. “It’s to put it in the hands of our creators … to create these incredible and immersive stories.”

During the demo day at Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, California, Promise CEO George Strompoulis explained to the media that the company — which bills itself as a generative AI studio developing movies, series and visual effects to “support human artistry” — is made up of four major components: Promise Studios can help produce “studio-quality features at a fraction of the cost and timeline”; then there’s the Muse AI technology platform workflow software; the Curious Refuge AI Filmmaking academy, to serve as “a pipeline of the best artists in the world” and to “upscale” existing film industry workers; and The Generation Company, which is Promise’s AI visual effects business.
Promise has done some testing with the Disney teams, and has a series pilot in production with another studio.

“I think it’s easy for people to have the misconception that there’s an AI button that could just make a movie,” said Rob Bredow, senior vice president of creative innovation at Disney. “That is not the approach that Disney’s taking; it’s not the approach that Promise is taking, which is why this has been a good collaboration.”
I watch the screens as the same woman from the cliff edge now appears to be crouching fearfully next to a blown-out car as explosions rain debris around her.

She’s still right in front of me, squatting next to those blue boxes in the Disney studio sound stage, camera trained on her. I also watch her pick up a screwdriver from the floor. On screen, it transforms into a mysterious scroll out of a Lara Croft-esque adventure movie.

“The ability to do this at cinematic-quality level is something that we’re at the beginning stages of now,” Clark said. “You not only need great filmmakers; you need creative technologists, you need artists who are masters in the AI tools.”

articles.headline: England scrap West Indies Test for red-ball Ashes prep at home
keyFacts: England has removed a Test match from its upcoming women's tour of the West Indies to prioritize red-ball preparation for the 2027 Ashes.
The West Indies tour will now consist of three one-day internationals and three T20 matches in April.
England will prepare for the June Ashes Test at Headingley with a training camp in India and several multi-day matches at home.
body: England scrap West Indies Test match with red-ball preparation ahead of Women's Ashes to take place at home

England's tour of West Indies in April will now comprise of three ODIs and as many T20 internationals; Women's Ashes Test at Headingley from June 24-27 will be preceded by four red-ball fixtures; four points available for winning Ashes Test in multi-format series
Wednesday 11 November 2026 14:15, UK
England have scrapped a women's Test match in West Indies this spring with the majority of their red-ball preparations ahead of the 2027 Ashes to take place at home.
Charlotte Edwards' side were due to play cricket in the Caribbean across all three formats in April but the tour will now consist of three one-day internationals and as many T20s.

An ECB statement read that there was "insufficient time to accommodate the Test match" as part of a tour that will begin after the first round of Metro Bank One Day Cup matches, during which all England players will be involved.

Exact dates will be released by Cricket West Indies in due course.
A four-day Test at Headingley from June 24-27 kicks off next summer's Women's Ashes, followed by three T20s and three ODIs in July.
What red-ball prep will England have?
England, who have not won a home women's Test since 2005 and not secured victory in the multi-format Ashes series since 2014, will head to India in January for a 10-day red-ball training camp.
A host of multi-day matches are then scheduled for the home summer.
Plans feature a three-dayer against Australia A in the run-up to the Ashes Test in Leeds and three best-vs-best, intra-squad matches in order to build competition for places.
ECB chief executive Richard Gould said: "We are all hugely excited by the prospect of England Women taking on Australia Women in their Ashes Test at Headingley.

"It will undoubtedly be one of the highlights of the summer and is worth four points in the multi-format series, so it is important that our players have the right preparation leading into the match and are given the best chance to succeed."
Gould added: "Best versus best in English conditions provides a valuable opportunity for the team.
"It also allows us to assess our strength in depth, give opportunities to more players and get a number of competitive multi-day cricket matches across a longer period into the wider group.
"We appreciate the constructive conversations with Cricket West Indies that have enabled us to look forward to an exciting tour of the Caribbean before focusing attentions back on our home summer."

articles.headline: Russia and Ukraine agree to a large exchange of prisoners of war, officials say
keyFacts: Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war during U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, officials said.
Russian delegation head Vladimir Medinsky and Ukrainian delegation head Rustem Umerov confirmed the planned release.
Jared Kushner said U.S. officials will meet Russian President Putin in Moscow on Thursday and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy in Dublin.
body: Russia and Ukraine agree to a large exchange of prisoners of war, officials say
ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Officials at U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine said Wednesday that the sides have agreed a large exchange of prisoners of war.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, said after the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi ended.
Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv's delegation in Abu Dhabi, confirmed the planned exchange.
Hopes were low for any major breakthrough in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped prisoners during their nearly five-year war.
U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.
Kushner says he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The context of the negotiations has changed since the last meeting in February in Geneva. The Trump administration has to reckon with Democrats, who could demand more support for Ukraine, taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections.
Also, Russia's wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.
Umerov said Kyiv's delegation is expected to meet Wednesday with European officials.

Moscow doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. However, representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi and were consulting with the Ukrainian delegation, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday's session was "constructive and quite substantive."
The talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including possible prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country, he said.
Security guarantees also were discussed, he said. However, Russia and Ukraine have shown no sign of a willingness to compromise on their demands.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the meeting "very productive," while cautioning that a breakthrough on stopping the war will take time.
The Abu Dhabi talks are being held against the backdrop of continued fighting on the front line, where little territory has changed hands this year.
Meanwhile, both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones.
Overnight, Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property.
Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to the regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko.
He said that the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of the main facilities for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers.

articles.headline: U.S. charges 3 men with plotting multiple terror attacks, including planned attack against U.K. airbase
keyFacts: U.S. authorities charged three men with plotting attacks against Jewish communities and a British military base housing American service members.
Officials alleged the defendants orchestrated the terror campaign for Iran-affiliated groups, with only Mohammad Al-Saadi currently in custody.
The indictment alleges the group conducted surveillance on RAF Fairford and gathered fuel and potential bomb materials for the plot.
body: Three men, including one already jailed in the U.S., were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in federal court in New York City.
Only Al-Saadi — an alleged pro-Iranian terrorist who is believed to have plotted attacks across Europe, Canada and the U.S., as first reported by NBC News — is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that Al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said McDonald, whose office is handling the case.
“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real,” he added in the statement.

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight Sept. 27 on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

The Justice Department indictment alleges that Al-Hassani paid associates to carry out surveillance of RAF Fairford in August and paid several people to move forward with the plot in September “by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel.”
The group even made custom decals to give the vans the appearance that they were used by a fuel company and a swimming pool supply business, authorities say.
Al-Hassani is alleged to have then tasked the people to go to the base with the fuel when U.K. law enforcement took the men into custody.

Al-Saadi was helping direct the RAF Fairford plot while he was in a U.S. prison, according to the indictment. He made video and phone calls to his family members in Iraq, who are alleged to have passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri.
In a July call with his sister, Al-Saadi asked, “What are we doing about all our old work?” — a reference to terrorist activity — according to investigators.
His sister replied, “It isn’t cancelled,” investigators said.

The indictment alleges that the three men conspired to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.
In June, Al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.
The U.S. government has designated Kata’ib Hizballah and the Revolutionary Guards as foreign terrorist organizations.
